resources.string: Learn
What is an IP address?

An IP address is the address of every device on the internet. When you open a website, the site sends its answer to this address, like a letter going to a home address.

You have two kinds of IP address. Your local IP is given by your router (for example 192.168.1.5) and only works inside your own network. Your public IP is given by your internet provider (ISP), and every website, ad network and app you use can see it.

A public IP does not reveal your name. But it shows which provider you use and roughly which city you are in, and it can link your activity across sites. Your provider knows who used which IP at any time.
IPv4 and IPv6

IPv4 and IPv6 are two versions of IP addresses, and your device can have both at once.

IPv4 looks like 203.0.113.42. There are about 4.3 billion IPv4 addresses, which is not enough for every device, so providers often share one public IPv4 address between many customers (CGNAT). This is very common on mobile data.

IPv6 looks like 2001:db8::1. There are practically unlimited IPv6 addresses, so your device can get its own public address.

If a VPN only protects IPv4, your IPv6 traffic can go outside the VPN and reveal your real address. That is why GetMyIP shows both addresses separately.
How does your IP change?

Your public IP changes in two ways: your provider gives you a new address, or your traffic leaves through another server.

Without any tools (this changes your address but does not hide you):
• Restart your router. Most home connections get a new address after reconnecting, unless you have a static IP.
• Switch between Wi-Fi and mobile data. Two networks, two public IPs.
• Turn airplane mode on and off. On mobile data you usually get a new address.

The new address still belongs to your provider, and your provider still knows who uses it.

With tools, your traffic leaves through another place: a VPN server or the Tor network. Websites see that address instead. Your provider only sees that you are connected to a VPN or Tor, not which sites you visit.

VPN or Tor?

With a VPN, you trust one company with all your traffic. With Tor, your traffic passes through three volunteer servers, and none of them knows both who you are and where you are going. Tor is usually slower.\n\nIf VPN or Tor connections are blocked on your network, Tor Browser and Orbot can connect using bridges.
